lessonTitle: Absorption and Distribution: Routes, Bioavailability and Volume of Distribution

blocks.text: A man with crushing chest pain is handed a nitrate tablet and told to let it dissolve under his tongue rather than swallow it. Within a minute or two the pain eases. Swallowed, the same drug would be largely destroyed by the liver before it ever reached his heart. Where a drug goes in, and where it goes next, decides whether it works at all.

blocks.markdown: **Pharmacokinetics** is what the body does to a drug. This unit covers the first two steps of ADME: **absorption** (how a drug gets from its site of administration into the blood) and **distribution** (how it spreads from the blood into the tissues). Two numbers summarise these steps: **bioavailability** (how much reaches the circulation) and **volume of distribution** (how widely it spreads).

blocks.title: Bioavailability (F)
blocks.text: Bioavailability, F, is the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. By definition an intravenous dose has F = 1 (100%) because it is placed directly into the blood. Any other route has F between 0 and 1.

blocks.caption: AUC is the area under the plasma concentration-time curve (mg.h/L), a measure of total drug exposure. Dividing each AUC by its dose allows different doses to be compared.

blocks.title: Calculating oral bioavailability from AUC
blocks.prompt: A drug is given as 100 mg orally, giving AUC = 12 mg.h/L. On another occasion 50 mg is given intravenously, giving AUC = 10 mg.h/L. Calculate the oral bioavailability. (Teaching example only.)

steps.text: Dose-normalise the oral AUC: 12 / 100 = 0.12 (mg.h/L per mg).
Dose-normalise the intravenous AUC: 10 / 50 = 0.20 (mg.h/L per mg).
Take the ratio of the two normalised values.
Interpret: 60% of the oral dose reaches the systemic circulation. The remaining 40% was either not absorbed from the gut or removed by first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver.

blocks.caption: Common routes of administration compared (general principles; exact values vary by drug and formulation).
rows: Bypasses absorption; irreversible once given; needs access
Venous drainage avoids the liver, so no first-pass effect; only small, lipid-soluble drugs
Large absorptive surface; useful for local lung and some systemic drugs
Depends on muscle blood flow; avoids first-pass
Absorption slower and steadier; avoids first-pass
Convenient; affected by gut absorption, food and first-pass metabolism
Partly avoids first-pass (lower rectum); useful if vomiting
Only potent lipid-soluble drugs; steady delivery over days

blocks.markdown: Once in the blood, a drug distributes between plasma and tissues. A drug that stays in the plasma has a small apparent volume; a drug that is taken up by fat, muscle or bound to tissue components leaves little in the plasma and has a large apparent volume. The **volume of distribution** captures this as a single number.

blocks.title: Volume of distribution (Vd)
blocks.text: Vd is the apparent volume of fluid that would be needed to contain the total amount of drug in the body at the same concentration as in plasma: Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration. It is a proportionality constant, not a real anatomical volume, and may greatly exceed total body water.

blocks.caption: For an IV bolus, C0 (mg/L) is the plasma concentration extrapolated back to time zero, i.e. as if distribution were instantaneous. Vd is in litres, or L/kg when divided by body mass.

blocks.title: Calculating volume of distribution
blocks.prompt: A 70 kg adult receives 280 mg of a drug by IV bolus (teaching example). The extrapolated plasma concentration at time zero is 4 mg/L. Calculate Vd in litres and in L/kg, and interpret it.

steps.text: Write the relationship and state the assumption: one-compartment behaviour, so the concentration at time zero reflects the whole dose in the volume.
Express per kilogram of body mass.
Interpret: total body water in a 70 kg adult is about 42 L, so 70 L exceeds it. The drug must be leaving the plasma and being taken up (bound or dissolved) in tissues.

blocks.answer: Vd = 70 L (1 L/kg), larger than total body water, indicating tissue uptake

blocks.title: What Vd tells you
blocks.text: A Vd of about 3 to 5 L means the drug is largely confined to plasma (often large or highly protein-bound molecules). About 14 L (roughly 0.2 L/kg) suggests extracellular fluid. Around 40 L suggests total body water. Values of several hundred litres mean extensive tissue binding, so little drug is in plasma and removal by dialysis is ineffective.

blocks.markdown: **Plasma protein binding.** Many drugs bind reversibly to plasma proteins: acidic drugs mainly to **albumin**, basic drugs to **alpha-1 acid glycoprotein**. Only the **unbound (free)** fraction can cross capillary walls, reach receptors, be metabolised or be filtered. Bound drug acts as a circulating reservoir. Highly bound drugs (for example warfarin, about 99% bound) tend to have a smaller Vd because more drug is held in the plasma. Binding is saturable and competitive, so two drugs can displace one another, and low albumin (for example in liver disease, nephrotic syndrome or malnutrition) raises the free fraction of acidic drugs.

items: Free drug is the pharmacologically active, diffusible fraction.
Bound drug is inactive while bound but is in rapid equilibrium with free drug.

A change in binding matters clinically mainly for highly bound (more than about 90%) drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, and often only transiently, because the freed drug is redistributed and eliminated.
Hypoalbuminaemia raises the free fraction, so a normal total level may hide a high free level.

blocks.title: Total versus free concentration
blocks.text: Laboratories usually report total drug concentration (bound plus free). In a patient with low albumin the total may look low or normal while the free, active concentration is raised, so interpret total levels with care.

points: Bioavailability F is the fraction of a dose reaching the systemic circulation; IV has F = 1, and oral F is reduced by incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism.
Route determines speed of onset: IV is immediate, sublingual, inhaled and IM are fast, oral is slowest.
Vd = Dose / C0 is an apparent volume; large values reflect tissue binding rather than a real space.
Only unbound drug is active and diffusible; extensive plasma protein binding restricts distribution and can be altered by displacement or low albumin.

questions.stem: Which statement about intravenous administration is correct?

options.text: It has a bioavailability of 100% by definition
It has the slowest onset of all routes
It is subject to first-pass hepatic metabolism
It depends on absorption from the gut wall

questions.correctOptionText: It has a bioavailability of 100% by definition

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the drug is delivered directly into the circulation so the whole dose is available.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: IV has the fastest onset because there is no absorption phase.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: IV drug enters the systemic circulation before reaching the liver, so it is not subject to first-pass metabolism.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: gut absorption applies to the oral route, not IV.

questions.explanation: An intravenous dose is placed directly in the bloodstream, so there is no absorption step and the entire dose reaches the systemic circulation. This is why IV administration is the reference against which the bioavailability of every other route is measured.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with an acute exacerbation of heart failure has marked gut oedema and is vomiting. His furosemide is changed from tablets to an injection. What is the best pharmacokinetic reason for this change?

options.text: IV delivery bypasses unreliable gut absorption and gives a rapid, predictable onset
IV drugs are not bound to plasma proteins
IV delivery increases the first-pass effect
IV delivery lowers the volume of distribution to zero

questions.correctOptionText: IV delivery bypasses unreliable gut absorption and gives a rapid, predictable onset

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bowel wall oedema and vomiting make oral absorption erratic; IV avoids this.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: protein binding is a property of the drug, not the route.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: IV avoids, rather than increases, first-pass metabolism.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: Vd is a property of the drug and patient, not the route, and is never zero.

questions.explanation: When gut absorption is unreliable (vomiting, intestinal oedema), the oral route gives unpredictable bioavailability and a delayed onset. The IV route removes the absorption step so the dose and onset are predictable.

questions.stem: A drug is given as a 150 mg IV bolus. The plasma concentration extrapolated back to time zero is 3 mg/L. Calculate the volume of distribution in litres.
questions.explanation: Vd = Dose / C0 = 150 mg / 3 mg/L = 50 L. This exceeds total body water in an adult, so the drug is distributed beyond the plasma into the tissues.

questions.stem: A 200 mg oral dose of a drug gives an AUC of 18 mg.h/L. A 100 mg IV dose of the same drug gives an AUC of 30 mg.h/L. Calculate the oral bioavailability as a fraction (between 0 and 1).
questions.explanation: Normalise each AUC to its dose: oral 18/200 = 0.09 and IV 30/100 = 0.30. The ratio 0.09/0.30 = 0.30, so 30% of the oral dose reaches the systemic circulation.

questions.stem: Drug X is 99% bound to albumin and drug Y is 50% bound to albumin. A second drug displaces 1% of each from albumin binding sites (so X becomes 98% bound and Y becomes 49% bound). Which statement best describes the immediate effect on free concentrations?

options.text: The free concentration of X doubles, while that of Y rises only slightly
The free concentration of Y doubles, while that of X is unchanged
Both free concentrations rise by exactly 1%
Neither free concentration changes because only bound drug is active

questions.correctOptionText: The free concentration of X doubles, while that of Y rises only slightly

distractorRationale.a: Correct: free fraction of X goes from 1% to 2%, doubling it; for Y it goes from 50% to 51%, a 2% rise.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: Y starts with a large free fraction, so a 1 point change is small in relative terms.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: the relative change depends on the starting free fraction, not on the absolute 1 point change.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: the free drug is the active fraction and it is the free fraction that changes.

questions.explanation: The free fraction of X rises from 1% to 2%, which is a doubling, whereas Y's free fraction rises from 50% to 51%, a 2% relative increase. This is why displacement matters most for very highly bound drugs, particularly if they have a narrow therapeutic index.

questions.stem: A drug given to a 70 kg adult has a calculated Vd of 600 L. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: The drug is extensively taken up by tissues, leaving only a small fraction in the plasma
The drug is restricted to the plasma compartment
The patient has 600 L of body fluid
The drug is highly protein bound in plasma and cannot reach tissues

questions.correctOptionText: The drug is extensively taken up by tissues, leaving only a small fraction in the plasma

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a Vd far above total body water means most drug sits outside the plasma, bound in tissues.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: a plasma-restricted drug would have a Vd of about 3 to 5 L.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: Vd is an apparent, not a physical, volume.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: high plasma protein binding tends to lower Vd, not raise it.

questions.explanation: Vd = amount in body / plasma concentration, so a very low plasma concentration relative to the body load yields a very large Vd. Since 600 L is far greater than any real body fluid space, it indicates extensive tissue binding or sequestration, for example in fat.

questions.stem: Compare the intravenous, sublingual and oral routes of administration in terms of speed of onset and bioavailability, explaining why oral bioavailability is often less than 100%.
markingGuide: IV: immediate onset, F = 1 (100%) as no absorption is needed
Sublingual: rapid onset because of rich mucosal blood supply, with venous drainage that avoids the liver and first-pass metabolism
Oral: slowest onset, bioavailability between 0 and 1
Reasons for reduced oral F: incomplete absorption (poor solubility, degradation in gut, efflux transporters)
Reason for reduced oral F: first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver via the portal circulation
questions.explanation: Route sets how directly a drug reaches the systemic circulation. Oral drugs must pass the gut wall and the portal vein and liver first, so some is lost, whereas IV and sublingual routes avoid these losses and act faster.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with cirrhosis has a serum albumin of 22 g/L (low) and is taking a highly albumin-bound drug at a standard dose. The laboratory reports a total drug concentration within the usual range. Explain why she may still be at risk of toxicity, and how plasma protein binding influences the distribution of a drug.
markingGuide: Only unbound (free) drug crosses membranes, reaches receptors and is active
Low albumin means fewer binding sites so a larger fraction of the drug is free
A normal total concentration (bound plus free) can therefore conceal an elevated free concentration
Highly bound drugs are held in plasma, restricting distribution (smaller Vd); lower binding allows more distribution into tissue
Binding is reversible and competitive, so displacement by other drugs can also raise free levels
Clinical consequence: increased effect or toxicity, particularly for narrow therapeutic index drugs; consider free level or dose reduction
questions.explanation: Total concentration includes bound drug that is pharmacologically inert. When albumin is low, the free fraction rises, so more drug is available at its target even though the total looks normal.

questions.stem: A 60 kg patient receives 90 mg of a drug by IV bolus (teaching example) and the extrapolated plasma concentration at time zero is 1.5 mg/L. Calculate the volume of distribution in L/kg.
questions.explanation: Vd = Dose / C0 = 90 / 1.5 = 60 L. Dividing by the body mass of 60 kg gives 1.0 L/kg.

questions.stem: True or false: drugs given by subcutaneous injection avoid first-pass hepatic metabolism.
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous drug is absorbed into capillaries that drain into the systemic venous circulation, not the portal vein, so it does not pass through the liver before reaching the body. Absorption is typically slower than by the intramuscular route but bioavailability is usually high.
